sections.h: Ben Sira: pride was not made for humans
sections.b:
Sirach 10 is the longest poem against pride outside the 66 books. "Why are dust and ashes proud?" (10:9) takes up Abraham's words (Genesis 18:27). A king today is dead tomorrow and inherits worms (10:10-11). "Human pride begins when a man turns away from the Lord / and his heart pulls away from the One who made him" (10:12). The Lord pulls down the thrones of rulers and plants the humble in their place (10:14-15), words close to Mary's song (Luke 1:52). "Arrogance was never made for mortals" (10:18).

At 10:13 Codex Vaticanus says "sin is where pride begins"; other witnesses and the Latin reverse it, "pride is the beginning of all sin." In that Latin form the line passed to Augustine (The City of God 14.13) and Thomas Aquinas (Summa Theologiae I-II, question 84, article 2), and so into Western teaching on pride as the root of sin.

common: Pride is the root or beginning of sin, a view Christians often support from Sirach 10:13 in its Latin form.
uncommon: In the Greek of Codex Vaticanus, Sirach 10:13 says the reverse: sin comes first, and pride grows from it.

sections.h: Ben Sira on friends old, false and tested
sections.b: Ben Sira returns to friendship again and again. A friend is not to be traded "for something that does not matter, / or a true brother for the gold of Ophir" (7:18). An old friend is like aged wine: "New friend, new wine: / give it time to age, and you will enjoy drinking it" (9:10), a comparison Jesus also makes (Luke 5:39). Good times do not reveal a friend, and in hard times even a friend may go off (12:8-9). The enemy who poses as a friend sweetens his words, weeps with his eyes, and trips you by the heel (12:16-17; compare Psalm 41:9). And not everyone should be told your heart (8:19).

sections.h: Prayer, alms and wise giving in Sirach 7 and 12
sections.b: Ben Sira joins prayer and alms: "Do not lose heart when you pray, / and do not overlook giving alms" (7:10). The Hebrew there has tsedaqah, "righteousness," already used for charity. After giving the priests their share, a person's blessing is complete only when he also reaches out to the poor (7:32), and kindness is owed even to the dead (7:33). In chapter 12 Ben Sira limits giving: "know who you are doing it for" (12:1), give to the godly and not to the sinner (12:4-7), lest the wicked use your bread against you. The Didache passes on a similar saying, "Let your alms sweat in your hands, until you know to whom you should give" (Didache 1:6).

Sirach 7:29-31 ties the honor of the priests to the great commandment: "Revere the Lord with all your soul, / and hold his priests in high regard. / With all your strength love the One who made you, / and do not desert the ones who serve him in worship" (7:29-30; compare Deuteronomy 6:5). Ben Sira lists the priests' portions from the Law: the guilt offering, "the gift of the shoulders" (the foreleg of Deuteronomy 18:3), the sacrifice of consecration and the first fruits (7:31). He writes as a loyal supporter of the temple of his day, a theme that culminates in his praise of Aaron, Phinehas and the high priest Simon (45:6-26; 50:1-21).

sections.h: The fear of the Lord as true honor (Sirach 9-10)
sections.b: For Ben Sira the fear of the Lord is the only sure ground of honor. "Let the fear of the Lord be what you boast in" (9:16). His riddle asks which race is honored, and answers: "Those who fear the Lord"; which is despised: "Those who break the commandments" (10:19). Among the rich, the honored and the poor, "the fear of the Lord is what they boast in" (10:22), and no nobleman, judge or ruler "is greater than the one who fears the Lord" (10:24). The Hebrew of 10:22 extends this to the sojourner, the stranger and the foreigner.

sections.h: Ben Sira's rich man who "found rest"
sections.b: Ben Sira warns that "gold has ruined many people / and bent the hearts of kings" (8:2), and that the rich man who says "I have found rest, / and now I will feast on my good things" does not know how soon he will leave them to others and die (11:18-19). The scene is close to Jesus' parable of the rich fool, who says to his soul, "Rest now. Eat, drink, celebrate" (Luke 12:19). Ben Sira also warns against the self-satisfied "I have all I need" (11:24; compare Revelation 3:17), and teaches that the Lord can make a poor man rich in a moment (11:21).

sections.h: Repayment on the day of death (Sirach 11)
sections.b: Ben Sira holds that God repays each person within this life, and if not sooner, then at its end: "it is easy for the Lord, on the day a person dies, / to pay him back for the way he has lived" (11:26). One hour of misery can blot out a lifetime of comfort, and a man's deeds come to light at his end (11:27). So, "Do not call anyone blessed until he has died" (11:28), advice the Greek historian Herodotus gives to Solon (Histories 1.32.7). The wicked will not go unpunished "right up to Hades" (9:12). The New Testament places a judgment after death (Hebrews 9:27).

Sirach 10:14 says, "The Lord has pulled down the thrones of rulers / and seated the gentle in their place," and 7:11 speaks of "One who brings low and lifts high." Mary's song uses the same verb and image: "He has pulled rulers down from thrones / and raised the lowly high" (Luke 1:52). Both draw on Hannah's song (1 Samuel 2:7-8). Ben Sira shows that this hope of reversal was part of Jewish prayer and teaching two centuries before Luke; whether Luke knew Sirach cannot be shown.

Ben Sira prizes a good wife: "Do not let a wise and good wife slip away from you, / for her graciousness is worth more than gold" (7:19), and tells a man with a wife he loves, "Do not drive her out" (7:26), the language of divorce. A father should give his daughter to "a man with good sense" (7:25). He warns husbands against jealousy that teaches "an evil lesson" (9:1) and against handing their soul over to a woman (9:2), and young men against other men's wives (9:9). The book speaks to men about women, in the outlook of its time.

sections.b: Ben Sira assumes slavery, but urges kindness: "Do not mistreat a servant who works honestly" (7:20), "Let your soul love a good servant, / and do not hold back his freedom" (7:21), in the spirit of the Law's release of slaves (Exodus 21:2; Deuteronomy 15:12-15). He also notes that "Free men will wait on a wise servant" (10:25), as Proverbs says a sensible servant may rule a disgraceful son (Proverbs 17:2). Elsewhere (30:33-40 in the Greek order) his advice about slaves is harsher.

Ben Sira warns, "Do not bring just anyone into your home, / for a cheat has many ways to set a trap" (11:29), and that a stranger settled in the house can "make you a stranger to your own household" (11:34). The rabbis quoted this advice from Ben Sira and approved it (Sanhedrin 100b; Yevamot 63b). It stands beside the Bible's call to welcome strangers (Genesis 18:1-8; Hebrews 13:2) as a word about discernment, not a refusal of help.

sections.h: Ben Sira's limit: "do not come to the aid of the sinner"
sections.b: Sirach 12:1-7 tells its reader to do good to the godly and not to help the sinner, who would use the gift against him, "For the Most High himself hates sinners" (12:6). Proverbs says, "If someone who hates you is hungry, feed him bread" (Proverbs 25:21), and Jesus commands, "keep loving your enemies, doing good" (Luke 6:35). Readers in churches that receive Sirach read 12:1-7 as prudence about funding wickedness; others see in it a real difference from Jesus' teaching.

sections.h: "Good and bad... come from the Lord" (Sirach 11)
sections.b: Ben Sira says the Lord's works are "full of wonder" and hidden (11:4), so kings sit on the ground and unknown men wear the crown (11:5). One man strains and falls behind while God lifts up another who is weak (11:11-13). "Good and bad, life and death, / poverty and wealth: they come from the Lord" (11:14), as Isaiah 45:7, Job 2:10 and Lamentations 3:38 also say. The "bad" is misfortune, not sin: Ben Sira later insists that God makes no one sin (15:11-20).
